title: EXISTS
description: Use EXISTS to test qualifying relationships without multiplying outer rows, with correlation, NULL, aggregate-subquery and multiple-witness examples.
notes:
## Test whether a qualifying relationship exists

EXISTS turns a subquery's row existence into a Boolean condition. It is true when the subquery produces at least one row and false when it produces none. This is useful when a report needs eligible outer entities rather than a list of every related record. For example, a library may want members who have at least one currently open loan.

Connect this topic with [subqueries in WHERE](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/subquery-in-where), [correlated subquery](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/correlated-subquery) and [anti join](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/anti-join). The examples use MySQL 8.4. Learn the row-existence meaning first; optimizer transformations may change the execution strategy without changing which outer rows meet that meaning.

## Build the qualifying subquery before negating anything

Suppose members stores one member per member_id and loans stores loan_id, member_id and state. A member qualifies when some loan refers to that member and has state open. The member relationship and state restriction both belong to the match definition. A closed loan alone does not establish that an open loan exists.

```sql
SELECT m.member_id, m.member_name
FROM members AS m
WHERE EXISTS (
 SELECT 1
 FROM loans AS l
 WHERE l.member_id = m.member_id
   AND l.state = 'open'
)
ORDER BY m.member_id;
```

The equality correlates the inner row with the current outer member. Without it, any open loan anywhere could make every member pass. A syntactically valid uncorrelated subquery can therefore answer a very different question. Name the roles with aliases and read the relationship predicate as a sentence before trusting a plausible-looking member list.

## Understand why the projected value is incidental

SELECT 1 is a common convention because the condition asks only whether a row exists. Selecting an actual column does not make EXISTS return that column to the outer query. Even selecting a null expression from an existing qualifying row does not make existence false: the row still exists. Missing projected values and absent rows are different concepts.

This distinction helps explain why EXISTS does not directly calculate a loan total or provide the most recent loan date. Those tasks need a measure or a selected related record. Use aggregation or a well-defined row-selection strategy when details are required. Do not expect EXISTS to return whichever inner value happens to be encountered first.

## Keep the outer grain stable

A member with four qualifying loans appears once when the outer members input contains that member once. EXISTS evaluates eligibility rather than projecting four member-loan pairs. A regular inner join would produce four appearances before any later aggregation or deduplication. If the task needs only eligible members, existence expresses that intention directly.

EXISTS does not impose uniqueness on an already duplicated outer relation. If an earlier join repeats a member, each repeated outer appearance can still pass. Establish the outer grain before assuming a semijoin-style condition has repaired earlier multiplication. Distinct member identities and distinct display names are also different concepts; two people can legitimately share a name.

## Distinguish existence from counting

If the question asks whether at least one loan exists, computing an exact count can express more work than the question requires. An optimizer may simplify suitable cases, so do not assume a universal performance difference based only on spelling. The clearest formulation is often the one that mirrors the requirement and makes the population explicit.

If the question instead asks for at least three open loans, simple EXISTS is insufficient. The threshold requires a grouped count or another correct counting strategy. Likewise, knowing that one loan exists says nothing about how many are overdue or how much debt is outstanding. Match the SQL construct to the information the caller actually requests.

## Handle null references and unknown attributes

Under ordinary equality, a loan whose member_id is null does not match a known member identity. Such a loan does not make every member eligible. A null state does not satisfy state equals open either. These results follow the stated relationship and eligibility rules; they should be covered by fixtures rather than inferred from fully populated sample rows.

A member can still pass when one loan is unknown and another is clearly open. Existence needs one qualifying witness, not complete knowledge about every inner row. Conversely, no visible qualifying witness does not necessarily prove that all real-world loans are closed. It establishes only that the supplied query population has no row satisfying the match.

## Compose independent requirements carefully

Suppose a campaign targets members with an open loan and an active reservation. Two EXISTS conditions express those separate relationships without multiplying loans by reservations. Each subquery must correlate with the same outer member. Accidentally correlating one to a different alias can make eligibility depend on another person's activity.

If one specific loan must satisfy two properties, put both properties on that same inner row. Two separate existence conditions can be witnessed by two different loans. For example, having some science-book loan and some overdue loan does not prove there is an overdue science-book loan. The difference is a useful introduction to quantifiers in everyday reporting.

## Recognize an aggregate subquery's row shape

An ungrouped aggregate normally returns one summary row even when its input is empty. Therefore EXISTS around SELECT COUNT(*) can be true even when the count is zero. EXISTS tests the summary row's presence, not whether the number inside it is positive. This is a common beginner error because the nested text visually mentions counting.

To test whether underlying rows exist, select from those rows with the qualifying predicates. To test a count threshold, express the threshold explicitly. A grouped aggregate behaves differently because it produces only represented groups, and HAVING can remove a summary row. Always reason about the subquery's output rows before applying the outer existence test.

## Negate existence with the same match definition

NOT EXISTS retains members with no qualifying open loan. It does not mean that they have never borrowed anything; members with only closed loans can qualify. A change in the inner predicate changes the absence condition. Keep that definition close to the query so a later author does not interpret the result more broadly than the SQL supports.

Unlike NOT IN over nullable output, this ordinary correlated formulation does not become globally unknown merely because an unrelated loan has a null member reference. The correlation decides whether each loan is a match. However, a poorly specified null-aware correlation can still alter the relationship, so negation is not a replacement for a precise schema and task contract.

## Verify eligibility with contrasting witnesses

A strong fixture includes one member with several open loans, one with only closed loans, one with no loans and one with a null state. Include two members sharing a name and an orphan null member reference. Check identities rather than display labels so duplicate names do not hide a missing correlation or accidental deduplication.

The beginner exercise selects members with an open loan. The intermediate exercise requires an open loan and an active reservation, using independent correlated conditions. These exercises test result semantics; they do not establish runtime performance. An index on the referenced member and relevant state may help, but representative execution plans are needed before making an optimization claim.

## Include visibility in the question

Existence is evaluated over rows visible to the query's execution context. A library report must retain its tenant and access restrictions. Returning only a yes-or-no decision can still reveal private borrowing activity. Do not treat the smaller projection as permission to query protected relations through an otherwise unauthorized boundary.

For any later write based on eligibility, evaluate concurrency and trusted enforcement separately. A member may return a book after a report is produced. EXISTS gives a clear relational observation, while transaction design determines how that observation can safely support an action. Keeping those responsibilities distinct makes the technique both easier to learn and safer to reuse. Review the candidate identity, qualifying relationship and observation time together whenever an existence condition drives a real action.

questions.question_text: When is EXISTS true?
options: When a selected number is positive only
When its subquery returns at least one row
questions.explanation: Existence concerns the presence of rows rather than the values projected from them.

questions.question_text: What does SELECT 1 conventionally signal inside EXISTS?
questions.explanation: The projected constant documents that inner details are unnecessary.

questions.question_text: What does the correlation l.member_id=m.member_id establish?
options: Every member belongs to every loan
The loan belongs to the candidate member
questions.explanation: The inner search must be tied to the current outer identity.

questions.question_text: What happens if that correlation is omitted?
options: Any open loan can qualify all outer members
questions.explanation: An uncorrelated existence condition has the same answer for every outer row.

questions.question_text: What if a qualifying row projects NULL?
questions.explanation: A row containing a null value is still a row.

questions.question_text: How many appearances does a unique outer member get from four witnesses?
questions.explanation: EXISTS tests eligibility without projecting each related pair.

questions.question_text: Does EXISTS fix already duplicated outer rows?
questions.explanation: Each existing outer appearance can independently pass the same condition.

questions.question_text: What is required for at least three open loans?
questions.explanation: One qualifying witness does not establish three.

questions.question_text: Does a null loan member reference match a known member with equality?
questions.explanation: Ordinary equality involving null does not establish a true relationship.

questions.question_text: Can one clear open loan qualify a member despite another unknown state?
options: No every state must be known
questions.explanation: An existential condition needs one qualifying witness.

questions.question_text: What do two independent EXISTS predicates permit?
options: Different rows to witness each requirement
questions.explanation: Separate existential requirements need not refer to the same related record.

questions.question_text: How require the same loan to be overdue and science-related?
options: Use two unrelated subqueries without correlation
Put both conditions on one inner loan row
questions.explanation: One combined predicate requires a single witness satisfying both properties.

questions.question_text: Why can EXISTS(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM empty_input) be true?
options: The aggregate returns a summary row
questions.explanation: EXISTS sees the summary row even when the count inside it is zero.

questions.question_text: Does NOT EXISTS open loans mean no borrowing history?
questions.explanation: Closed loans do not satisfy an open-loan match but still represent history.

questions.question_text: What output does EXISTS directly provide?
questions.explanation: Related details require additional projection or aggregation beyond the existence test.

questions.question_text: Which fixture exposes missing correlation?
options: Every member has one identical open loan
Only one member and one loan
Several members but only one has an open loan
questions.explanation: An uncorrelated predicate would incorrectly include members lacking the relationship.

questions.question_text: Can an unrelated null inner reference poison ordinary NOT EXISTS globally?
options: Yes every null invalidates all candidates
questions.explanation: Each inner row is tested against the current correlation rather than a nullable NOT IN set.

questions.question_text: What supports an actual performance claim?
questions.explanation: The optimizer can transform equivalent constructs, so plans and measurements matter.

questions.question_text: Does a Boolean result eliminate privacy concerns?
options: Yes because no detail columns are returned
questions.explanation: Even relationship existence can reveal protected activity.

questions.question_text: Can a later return of a book change the business observation?
options: No EXISTS locks the fact forever
Only if the member is renamed
questions.explanation: The statement observes a data state; later actions need their own concurrency contract.

coding_problems.title: Find members with an open loan
coding_problems.task: Return member_id,member_name for members with at least one open loan. Order by member_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE members(member_id INT PRIMARY KEY,member_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE loans(loan_id INT PRIMARY KEY,member_id INT NULL,state VARCHAR(10) NULL); CREATE TABLE reservations(reservation_id INT PRIMARY KEY,member_id INT NOT NULL,state VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO members VALUES (1,'Ari'),(2,'Ari'),(3,'Kim'),(4,'Jo'); INSERT INTO loans VALUES (1,1,'open'),(2,1,'open'),(3,2,'closed'),(4,3,'open'),(5,NULL,'open'),(6,4,NULL); INSERT INTO reservations VALUES (1,1,'cancelled'),(2,3,'active'),(3,3,'active');
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT m.member_id,m.member_name FROM members AS m WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans AS l WHERE l.member_id=m.member_id AND l.state='open') ORDER BY m.member_id;

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO members VALUES (1,'A'); INSERT INTO loans VALUES (1,NULL,'open');

coding_problems.title: Require an open loan and active reservation
coding_problems.task: Return member_id for members with at least one open loan and at least one active reservation. Order by member_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE members(member_id INT PRIMARY KEY,member_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE loans(loan_id INT PRIMARY KEY,member_id INT NULL,state VARCHAR(10) NULL); CREATE TABLE reservations(reservation_id INT PRIMARY KEY,member_id INT NOT NULL,state VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO members VALUES (1,'Ari'),(2,'Ari'),(3,'Kim'),(4,'Jo'); INSERT INTO loans VALUES (1,1,'open'),(2,1,'open'),(3,2,'closed'),(4,3,'open'),(5,NULL,'open'),(6,4,NULL); INSERT INTO reservations VALUES (1,1,'cancelled'),(2,3,'active'),(3,3,'active');
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT m.member_id FROM members AS m WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans AS l WHERE l.member_id=m.member_id AND l.state='open') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reservations AS r WHERE r.member_id=m.member_id AND r.state='active') ORDER BY m.member_id;

options: The first row of the subquery
TRUE or FALSE based on whether any row is returned
NULL if zero rows are returned
original_questions.explanation: EXISTS is a pure boolean test of row presence.

original_questions.question_text: Inside an EXISTS subquery, what do the selected columns matter for?
options: They determine the final output columns
Nothing — only row existence matters, so SELECT 1 or SELECT * behave the same
They must match the outer SELECT list
original_questions.explanation: EXISTS discards the actual selected values; it only checks whether any row came back.

original_questions.question_text: Using the sample data, why does the department 'HR' get excluded from `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.department = d.name)`?
options: No employee has department = 'HR', so the subquery returns zero rows there
HR is spelled differently in the departments table
EXISTS always excludes the last row
original_questions.explanation: No employee row matches department 'HR', so the correlated subquery is empty and EXISTS is FALSE.

original_questions.question_text: Why can EXISTS be more efficient than IN with a large multi-row subquery?
options: EXISTS can short-circuit and stop at the first matching row
EXISTS is always evaluated at compile time
original_questions.explanation: EXISTS only needs to find one matching row to be satisfied, unlike building a full membership set.

original_questions.question_text: Can EXISTS ever evaluate to NULL or UNKNOWN?
options: Yes, when the subquery has NULLs
No — EXISTS is always definitively TRUE or FALSE
Yes, when the subquery returns zero rows
original_questions.explanation: Unlike value comparisons, EXISTS only checks row presence, so it never produces UNKNOWN.

original_questions.question_text: Is `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees)` with no outer reference a valid, if usually not very useful, query?
options: Yes — it's valid, it just answers "is the table non-empty" once for the whole query
original_questions.explanation: An uncorrelated EXISTS is legal SQL, just a less powerful use of the construct.

original_questions.question_text: What is the real power of EXISTS most associated with?
options: Correlation — testing per outer row whether a related row exists
original_questions.explanation: EXISTS shines when correlated, checking existence per outer row against related data.

original_questions.question_text: Which best describes why `SELECT 1` is conventional inside EXISTS rather than `SELECT column`?
options: It's required by the SQL standard
It's a style signal that only row presence matters; engines typically skip fetching data for EXISTS regardless
It runs faster because 1 is an integer
original_questions.explanation: It's a readability convention, not a hard requirement — the actual selected values are irrelevant to EXISTS.
